course.title: Digital Marketing Masterclass

lessons.body:
Marketing Fundamentals

Marketing is how a business finds people who need what it sells, shows them why it is worth buying, and keeps them coming back. Digital marketing does all of that online — through search engines, social media, email and ads — where customers can be reached, measured and re-targeted far more cheaply than with print or TV.

Every marketing plan rests on the 4 Ps: Product (what you sell and why it is useful), Price (what it costs and what that price signals), Place (where customers find it — a shop, a website, an app) and Promotion (how you tell people about it). Change one P and the others shift too: a premium price needs premium promotion and a place that feels premium.

Good marketing starts with knowing the audience. A buyer persona is a short profile of your ideal customer — age, job, problems, where they spend time online — built from real research, not guesses. A shop selling running shoes to college students markets very differently from one selling them to marathon runners, even though the product is the same.

Buyer persona: "Priya, 21, B.Tech student in Warangal"
- Problem: needs affordable running shoes that last a semester
- Where she is online: Instagram reels, YouTube reviews
- What convinces her: student discount + honest review video
- Marketing move: Instagram reel + 10% student offer

Step by step: pick one audience, learn where they spend time online, match one of the 4 Ps to their biggest problem, and measure whether they act — clicks, sign-ups or sales.

  • Key points
  • Marketing connects a product with the people who need it; digital marketing does it online, where results can be measured.
  • The 4 Ps are Product, Price, Place and Promotion — change one and the others shift.
  • A buyer persona is a research-based profile of your ideal customer; market to the persona, not to everyone.

options: To make a website look pretty
To reach the right people online, show them why a product is worth buying, and measure the result
To post on social media every day
To spend as much as possible on ads
mcqs.q: What is the main goal of digital marketing?
mcqs.why: Digital marketing is about reaching the right audience online, persuading them, and measuring clicks, sign-ups or sales so you know what worked.

mcqs.q: Which of these are the 4 Ps of marketing?
mcqs.why: The classic marketing mix is Product (what you sell), Price (what it costs), Place (where customers find it) and Promotion (how you tell them).

options: A short profile of your ideal customer, built from real research
A celebrity who promotes your product
mcqs.q: What is a buyer persona?
mcqs.why: A buyer persona describes your ideal customer — their age, problems and where they spend time online — so marketing speaks to real people, not everyone.

options: Place and Promotion, so the shop and its ads feel premium too
mcqs.q: A shop raises its price to signal premium quality. Which other P must change to match?
mcqs.why: The 4 Ps work together: a premium price needs a premium-feeling place to buy and premium promotion, or customers will not believe the price.

options: Every click, sign-up and sale can be tracked, so you know exactly what worked
mcqs.q: Why is digital marketing easier to measure than a newspaper ad?
mcqs.why: Online, each click, sign-up and purchase is recorded, so a marketer can see which channel and message actually produced results.

tasks.answer: Promotion is the fourth P: how you tell people about the product — ads, social media, email and offers.
tasks.hint: Which P covers advertising and telling people about the product?

lessons.body:
SEO Essentials

SEO (Search Engine Optimisation) is the work of making a page show up high in Google's free (organic) results when people search for something it covers. When someone searches "best budget laptop for students", Google ranks pages by relevance and quality — SEO is how you earn a top spot instead of paying for an ad.

Three parts matter. On-page SEO is what you control on the page: a clear title tag, one main heading, the search phrase used naturally in the text, a short meta description that invites the click, and fast loading. Technical SEO is the plumbing: the page works on mobile, loads quickly, and has no broken links. Off-page SEO is mostly backlinks — other trusted sites linking to yours, which Google reads as votes of confidence.

Start with keyword research: find the exact words people type. A new blog should target specific, low-competition phrases ("best laptop under 40000 for students") rather than fighting giants for "laptop". Then write the best answer to that search — genuinely useful content wins over keyword stuffing, which Google now penalises.

Title tag (shows as the blue link in Google):
  Best Budget Laptops for Students in India 2026 | LearnHub
Meta description (the grey text under it):
  Compare 10 student laptops under Rs. 40,000 - battery,
  weight and performance tested. Find your pick in 5 minutes.

Step by step: pick one search phrase, check what already ranks for it, write a better page with a clear title and meta description, make it fast and mobile-friendly, then earn links by sharing it where your audience is.

  • Key points
  • SEO earns free traffic from search results; it is not paid advertising.
  • On-page SEO (title, headings, meta description), technical SEO (speed, mobile) and off-page SEO (backlinks) all matter.
  • Target specific search phrases and write the genuinely best answer — keyword stuffing is penalised.

mcqs.q: What does SEO stand for?
mcqs.why: SEO is Search Engine Optimisation: improving a page so it ranks higher in a search engine's free results.

options: SEO traffic is free (organic) ranking you earn; paid ads cost money per click
SEO only works on social media
Paid ads appear below organic results
mcqs.q: What is the difference between SEO traffic and paid search ads?
mcqs.why: Organic results are earned by relevance and quality and cost nothing per click; ads are paid placements, usually marked Sponsored.

options: The first line of the article
The text that appears as the clickable blue link in search results
mcqs.q: What is the title tag of a page?
mcqs.why: The title tag is what Google shows as the blue clickable headline for a result, so it should contain the search phrase and invite the click.

options: A link back to the home page
A link from another website to yours, which search engines treat as a vote of confidence
A link hidden in the footer
mcqs.q: What is a backlink?
mcqs.why: Backlinks from trusted sites signal to Google that your page is worth ranking; more quality backlinks usually mean higher rankings.

options: Short phrases are banned by Google
Specific phrases have less competition and match what real searchers want, so a new site can actually rank
mcqs.q: Why should a new blog target a specific phrase like "best laptop under 40000 for students" instead of just "laptop"?
mcqs.why: Broad words like "laptop" are fought over by huge sites; specific phrases have weaker competition and clearer searcher intent.

tasks.answer: The title tag is the clickable headline Google shows for a result; a good one contains the search phrase and invites the click.
tasks.code: The text that appears as the clickable blue link in search results is the ___
tasks.hint: Which HTML element becomes the blue headline in Google results?
tasks.prompt: Complete the sentence about what searchers see first.
tasks.title: Fill in the blank

lessons.body:
Social Media Strategy

Social media marketing is not posting at random — it is a strategy: pick the platforms your audience actually uses, post content they value, and turn attention into followers, sign-ups or sales. A B2B software company belongs on LinkedIn; a fashion brand for teenagers belongs on Instagram Reels.

Content falls into three buckets that keep a feed healthy: educate (tips, how-tos, explainers), entertain (behind-the-scenes, trends, humour) and promote (offers, launches, testimonials). A good rule is roughly 80% value and 20% promotion — feeds that only sell get unfollowed fast.

Measure what matters with engagement rate: (likes + comments + shares) divided by reach, times 100. Reach tells you how many people saw a post; engagement tells you how many cared enough to act. A post seen by 10,000 people with 500 interactions has a 5% engagement rate — far more useful than follower count alone.

Engagement rate = (likes + comments + shares) / reach x 100
Example: (350 likes + 100 comments + 50 shares) / 10,000 reach
       = 500 / 10,000 x 100 = 5%
Content mix: 80% educate/entertain, 20% promote

Step by step: choose one platform where your audience lives, plan a week of posts across the three buckets, publish at the times your audience is online, and each week keep what got engagement and drop what did not.

  • Key points
  • Pick platforms by where your audience is, not by what is trendy.
  • Mix educate, entertain and promote content — about 80% value, 20% promotion.
  • Engagement rate ((likes + comments + shares) / reach x 100) measures real interest better than follower count.

options: Picking the platforms your audience actually uses
mcqs.q: What is the first step of a social media strategy?
mcqs.why: Strategy starts with audience fit: a B2B company belongs on LinkedIn, a teen fashion brand on Instagram — posting where your audience is not wastes effort.

mcqs.q: What are the three content buckets in a healthy social media feed?
mcqs.why: Educate (tips, how-tos), entertain (behind-the-scenes, trends) and promote (offers, launches) keep a feed valuable; about 80% should be value, 20% promotion.

options: Likes + comments + shares, divided by reach, times 100
mcqs.q: How is engagement rate calculated?
mcqs.why: Engagement rate = (likes + comments + shares) / reach x 100. It shows what share of viewers cared enough to interact.

mcqs.q: A post reaches 10,000 people and gets 500 likes, comments and shares in total. What is its engagement rate?
mcqs.why: 500 / 10,000 x 100 = 5%. Reach is the denominator because it counts the people who actually saw the post.

options: Followers who never see or interact with posts add no value; reach and engagement show real attention
Followers do not use social media
mcqs.q: Why is follower count alone a weak measure of success?
mcqs.why: A big follower count means little if posts reach few people and nobody interacts; engagement rate measures the attention that actually happens.

tasks.code:
likes = 350
comments = 100
shares = 50
reach = 10000
engagement_rate = (likes + comments + shares) / reach * 100
tasks.hint: Add up all the interactions first, then divide by reach and multiply by 100.
tasks.prompt: A post reaches 10,000 people and gets 350 likes, 100 comments and 50 shares. What is its engagement rate?
tasks.title: Predict the result

lessons.body:
Email Campaigns

Email marketing is sending useful, wanted messages to people who asked to hear from you — newsletters, offers, course updates. It is still one of the highest-return channels in marketing because the list is yours: no algorithm decides who sees it, and every send can be measured.

Two numbers decide whether a campaign works. The open rate is opens divided by delivered emails, times 100 — it mostly measures your subject line. The click-through rate (CTR) is clicks divided by delivered emails, times 100 — it measures whether the email's content was worth acting on. A 20% open rate with a 2% CTR is a normal, healthy result for most lists.

Never buy an email list or add people without permission — that is spam, it is illegal in many countries, and it destroys deliverability: providers start sending your mail to the spam folder. Build the list honestly with a signup form and a clear reason to join, and always include an unsubscribe link.

Delivered: 2,000 emails
Opened: 400  -> open rate = 400 / 2,000 x 100 = 20%
Clicked: 60  -> CTR = 60 / 2,000 x 100 = 3%
Subject line test: A "Your 10% student offer ends tonight"
                   B "LearnHub newsletter #12"  (A usually wins)

Step by step: grow the list with a signup form, write a subject line that promises one clear benefit, keep the email short with one clear call to action, then check open rate and CTR and test one change at a time.

  • Key points
  • Email marketing works because the list is yours — no algorithm gates who sees it.
  • Open rate (opens / delivered x 100) tests the subject line; CTR (clicks / delivered x 100) tests the content.
  • Never buy lists or mail people without permission — it is spam and kills deliverability.

options: Opens divided by delivered emails, times 100
mcqs.q: What is the open rate of an email campaign?
mcqs.why: Open rate = opens / delivered x 100. It mainly measures how good the subject line and sender name were.

options: How fast the email was sent
Clicks divided by delivered emails, times 100 — whether the content was worth acting on
How many people opened the email twice
The size of the email list
mcqs.q: What does click-through rate (CTR) measure?
mcqs.why: CTR = clicks / delivered x 100. It shows whether the email's content and call to action persuaded readers to click.

mcqs.q: 2,000 emails are delivered and 400 are opened. What is the open rate?
mcqs.why: 400 / 2,000 x 100 = 20%. A 20% open rate is a normal, healthy result for most lists.

options: Those people never asked to hear from you, so it is spam — it is illegal in many places and harms deliverability
Bought lists have no email addresses
Bought lists only work on weekends
mcqs.q: Why should a marketer never buy an email list?
mcqs.why: Mailing people without permission is spam; providers notice the complaints and start sending your mail to the spam folder, and it breaks the law in many countries.

mcqs.q: Which subject line is most likely to get opened?
mcqs.why: A good subject line promises one clear, specific benefit with urgency — an offer ending tonight — while generic subjects like "Newsletter #12" promise nothing.

tasks.answer: 400 / 2,000 x 100 = 20% — a normal, healthy open rate.
tasks.hint: Divide opened by delivered, then multiply by 100.
tasks.prompt: 2,000 emails are delivered and 400 are opened. What is the open rate?
tasks.title: Predict the result

lessons.body:
Google Analytics Basics

Google Analytics (GA4) is a free tool that records what happens on your website: how many people visit, where they come from, which pages they read, and whether they buy or sign up. Without it, marketing is guesswork — with it, every channel can be judged by real numbers.

Learn four terms. A user is a person visiting your site. A session is one visit — a user can have many sessions, and one session can include many pageviews. A pageview is one load of one page. A conversion is the action you want — a purchase, a signup, a form submit — and you must tell GA4 which event counts as one.

Traffic sources tell you where visitors come from: organic search (Google), social (Instagram, LinkedIn), direct (typed the URL), referral (a link on another site) and paid (ads). Add UTM parameters to links in campaigns — ?utm_source=instagram&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=student-offer — so GA4 shows exactly which post or email brought each visitor.

UTM-tagged link (paste into a campaign post or email):
https://learnhub.example/courses/python
  ?utm_source=instagram&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=student-offer
GA4 then reports: source = instagram, medium = social,
campaign = student-offer - so you know that post worked.

Step by step: install GA4 on the site, set up one conversion event (e.g. course enrolment), tag every campaign link with UTM parameters, then weekly compare channels by sessions and conversions — spend more where conversions are cheapest.

  • Key points
  • GA4 is free and records visitors, sessions, pageviews and conversions.
  • A session is one visit; one user can have many sessions, and one session can include many pageviews.
  • UTM parameters tag campaign links so GA4 shows exactly which post or email brought each visitor.

options: Recording what happens on a website — visitors, sources, pages and conversions — so marketing can be judged by real numbers
mcqs.q: What is Google Analytics mainly used for?
mcqs.why: GA4 tracks who visits, where they came from, what they do and whether they convert, turning marketing from guesswork into measurement.

options: A user account on the site
One visit to the website, which can include many pageviews
mcqs.q: What is a session in Google Analytics?
mcqs.why: A session is one visit. One user can have many sessions, and one session can contain many pageviews as they browse.

options: The action you want a visitor to take — a purchase, signup or form submit — which you define in GA4
mcqs.q: What is a conversion?
mcqs.why: A conversion is the goal action (purchase, signup, enrolment). You tell GA4 which event counts, then it reports how many happened and from which channel.

options: They tag campaign links so analytics shows exactly which post, email or ad brought each visitor
They block bots from the site
mcqs.q: What do UTM parameters do?
mcqs.why: UTM tags like utm_source=instagram and utm_campaign=student-offer travel with the link, so GA4 can attribute each visit to the exact campaign.

options: Google Ads, because ads are paid
Instagram, because it converted 5% of sessions versus 1% for ads
Neither — sessions are all that matter
mcqs.q: Your Instagram campaign brings 1,000 sessions and 50 signups; your Google Ads bring 1,000 sessions and 10 signups. Which channel performed better?
mcqs.why: Conversions decide performance, not sessions: Instagram converted 50/1,000 = 5%, Ads only 10/1,000 = 1%.

tasks.answer: A session is one visit. One user can have many sessions, and a session can include many pageviews.
tasks.code: A ___ is a single visit to your website, which can include many pageviews.
tasks.hint: Which GA4 term means one visit?
tasks.prompt: Complete the sentence about visits to a website.
tasks.title: Fill in the blank

Content Marketing & Copywriting

Content marketing is earning attention by publishing genuinely useful material — guides, videos, templates — instead of interrupting people with ads. A student who finds your free "Python cheat sheet" trusts you, and trust is what later turns into an enrolment. Copywriting is the craft inside it: choosing the exact words that make someone act.

Good copy follows a simple shape. A headline promises one clear benefit ("Learn Python in 30 days — no experience needed"). The body proves it in short, specific sentences — numbers and examples beat adjectives. And a call to action (CTA) tells the reader exactly what to do next: "Start learning free", not the vague "Click here".

Write for one reader, not a crowd. "You" beats "users", active verbs beat passive ones ("Build your first app today" beats "Your first app can be built today"), and every claim should be checkable. Then test: run two headlines, keep the one more people click — that is A/B testing, and it applies to subject lines, buttons and landing pages alike.

Weak headline:  "Welcome to our Python course page"
Strong headline: "Learn Python in 30 days - no experience needed"
Weak CTA:  "Click here"
Strong CTA: "Start learning free - no card needed"

Step by step: pick one reader and one problem, promise the benefit in the headline, prove it with specifics in the body, end with one clear call to action, then A/B test the headline against another version.

  • Key points
  • Content marketing earns attention with useful material; copywriting chooses the words that make people act.
  • Good copy = headline promising one benefit + specific body + one clear call to action.
  • Write for one reader, use "you" and active verbs, and A/B test headlines and CTAs.

options: Earning attention by publishing genuinely useful material instead of interrupting people with ads
Posting the same ad on every platform
mcqs.q: What is content marketing?
mcqs.why: Content marketing attracts people with useful guides, videos or templates; the trust it builds later turns into sales or signups.

options: A phone call to a customer
A clear instruction telling the reader exactly what to do next, such as "Start learning free"
mcqs.q: What is a call to action (CTA)?
mcqs.why: A CTA is the explicit next step — "Start learning free", "Buy now" — and vague ones like "Click here" convert far worse.

options: "Learn Python in 30 days — no experience needed"
mcqs.q: Which headline is strongest?
mcqs.why: It promises one clear, specific benefit with a time frame and removes the main fear (no experience needed); the others promise nothing.

options: It speaks directly to one reader and makes the action clear, which converts better than vague, passive wording
mcqs.q: Why does good copy use "you" and active verbs?
mcqs.why: Direct, active copy ("Build your first app today") feels personal and tells the reader what to do; passive, generic copy does neither.

options: Running two versions of a headline, button or page and keeping the one more people act on
Grading a campaign A or B
Testing a website on two browsers
mcqs.q: What is A/B testing in marketing?
mcqs.why: A/B testing compares two versions with real users and keeps the winner — it applies to headlines, subject lines, buttons and landing pages.

tasks.answer: A call to action (CTA) is the explicit next step for the reader; "Start learning free" is specific, while "Click here" is vague.

tasks.hint: Which three-word term is shortened to CTA?
tasks.prompt: Complete the sentence about telling the reader what to do next.
